21259.title: Elementary Algebra
21259.heading: Elementary Algebra
21259.content:
Parent topic: [[Mathematics]]

Elementary Algebra organizes the number systems, symbolic forms, operations, equations, and inequalities that generalize arithmetic. It is a chapter-tier topic, so Full Notes link to its focused child tags instead of directly to this page.

21260.title: Elementary Algebra
21260.heading: Elementary Algebra > Overview Chapter
21260.content: Elementary algebra begins with a change in viewpoint. Arithmetic evaluates operations on particular numbers, while algebra uses symbols to express relationships that remain true across many possible values. A letter may stand for an arbitrary number, an unknown to be found, or a quantity that varies with a situation. This symbolic language makes it possible to state general properties, simplify complicated calculations, and translate practical relationships into equations or inequalities. The subject is cumulative: reliable symbolic work depends on the properties of numbers and operations, and later solution methods depend on understanding expressions.

21261.title: Elementary Algebra
21261.heading: Elementary Algebra > Overview Chapter > Numbers and the laws of arithmetic
21261.content:
[[Number Systems and Arithmetic]] establishes the objects and structural laws that algebra generalizes. Natural numbers support counting and ordering, integers add opposites so subtraction can remain within a number system, rational numbers add quotients of integers, and irrational numbers complete the real-number line beyond fractional representation. A number line connects order with position and makes absolute value interpretable as distance from zero.

Operations have properties that justify symbolic rearrangement. Closure asks whether an operation stays within a set. An identity element leaves a value unchanged. Commutativity permits a change in order, associativity permits a change in grouping, and distributivity connects multiplication with addition. These properties are not decorative labels: combining like terms, expanding products, factoring expressions, and preserving equality all depend on them. Knowing which operations lack a property is equally important; subtraction and division, for example, are not commutative.

21262.title: Elementary Algebra
21262.heading: Elementary Algebra > Overview Chapter > Fractions and decimal representation
21262.content:
[[Fractions and Decimal Forms]] extends division beyond the natural numbers. A fraction records a numerator divided by a nonzero denominator. Different numerator-denominator pairs can represent the same point on the number line, so the cancellation law explains equivalent fractions and reduction to lowest terms. Addition and subtraction require a common denominator, while multiplication acts directly on numerators and denominators. Division becomes multiplication by the reciprocal.

Decimal form connects fractions to positional notation. A rational number has a decimal expansion that terminates or repeats, and a repeating decimal can be converted back to a fraction by aligning and subtracting repeated tails. An irrational number instead has an infinite nonrepeating expansion. These representations show why exact equality must be distinguished from approximation: a short decimal can approximate an irrational quantity without becoming equal to it.

21263.title: Elementary Algebra
21263.heading: Elementary Algebra > Overview Chapter > Reading and simplifying expressions
21263.content:
[[Algebraic Expressions]] treats an expression as a structured combination of numbers, variables, operations, and grouping symbols. Its terms are separated by addition or subtraction, and numerical coefficients scale their variable parts. Like terms have identical variable factors and exponents, so the distributive property permits their coefficients to be combined. Unlike terms cannot be merged merely because they occur in the same expression.

Evaluation substitutes specified values for variables and then follows the grouping and operation structure. Simplification produces an equivalent form by suppressing parentheses correctly, distributing factors, and combining like terms. Translation works in the other direction: verbal relationships such as a sum, difference, product, quotient, square, or reciprocal become symbolic expressions. The important discipline is preserving order and grouping rather than translating one word at a time without regard to the relationship described.

21264.title: Elementary Algebra
21264.heading: Elementary Algebra > Overview Chapter > Exponents, powers, and inverse operations
21264.content:
[[Exponents and Roots]] gives concise notation for repeated multiplication and its reversal. In a power, the base is the repeated factor and the exponent records how many copies occur. The laws of exponents follow from this meaning: multiplying powers with a common base adds exponents, division subtracts them when the base is nonzero, a power raised to a power multiplies exponents, and a power of a product distributes the exponent across its factors.

Zero and negative exponents extend the pattern consistently. A nonzero base to the zero power equals one, while a negative exponent denotes the reciprocal of the corresponding positive power. Roots reverse exponentiation: a square root is a number whose square gives the radicand, and a cube root is a number whose cube does so. The notation is compact, but parentheses remain crucial because the square of a negative number differs from the negative of a square.

21265.title: Elementary Algebra
21265.heading: Elementary Algebra > Overview Chapter > Finding and expressing patterns
21265.content:
[[Sequences and Algebraic Patterns]] uses variables to replace a list of separate cases with a general term. A sequence has an ordered position, and a law of formation explains how its values are produced. An arithmetic progression changes by a constant difference, giving a linear formula for the term at position (n). A geometric progression changes by a constant ratio, giving an exponential formula.

Pattern recognition in algebra is not a guess detached from evidence. A proposed general term must reproduce the listed cases and explain the operation that advances from one position to the next. Pairing terms from opposite ends of an arithmetic sequence also exposes a constant pair sum, turning a long addition into a short product. These methods show algebra functioning as a language for regularity.

21266.title: Elementary Algebra
21266.heading: Elementary Algebra > Overview Chapter > Polynomials and rational expressions
21266.content:
[[Polynomial and Rational Expressions]] applies the laws of arithmetic to expressions built from powers and coefficients. Monomials contain one term, binomials two, and trinomials three. Polynomial multiplication distributes every term of one factor across every term of the other and then combines like terms. The FOIL mnemonic is a special case for two binomials, not a separate law.

Polynomial long division repeats a cycle: divide leading terms, multiply the divisor, subtract, and continue until the remainder has lower degree than the divisor. Rational expressions are quotients of algebraic expressions and are undefined wherever their denominator is zero. They are simplified by factoring and cancelling common factors, added through common denominators, and divided by multiplying by a reciprocal. Cancellation removes factors, not arbitrary terms joined by addition.

21267.title: Elementary Algebra
21267.heading: Elementary Algebra > Overview Chapter > Factoring and reusable identities
21267.content:
[[Factoring and Algebraic Identities]] reverses expansion by expressing a sum as a product. The first step is often to remove the greatest factor common to every term. When no factor spans the full expression, grouping can expose a repeated binomial factor. Quadratic trinomials can be factored by finding numbers whose product and sum match the required coefficients.

Special identities make recurring structures immediately recognizable. The square of a sum or difference produces two square terms and a doubled product. A difference of squares factors into conjugate binomials. Sums and differences of cubes use a linear factor paired with a quadratic factor. These identities support exact mental calculations, multi-stage factorization, and equation solving. A complete factorization may require applying more than one pattern in sequence.

21268.title: Elementary Algebra
21268.heading: Elementary Algebra > Overview Chapter > Linear equations and modeling
21268.content:
[[Linear Equations and Modeling]] distinguishes an equation that is true only for particular values from an algebraic identity true for all permissible values. Solving an equation means finding values that make both sides equal. Valid transformations preserve the balance: adding equal quantities to both sides or multiplying both sides by the same nonzero quantity produces an equivalent equation.

Linear equations isolate an unknown whose highest power is one. Fractions may be removed by multiplying through by a common denominator, and proportions may be solved through cross multiplication when denominators are nonzero. A proposed solution is verified by substitution into the original equation. For word problems, the central work occurs before manipulation: assign a variable, express related quantities consistently, build the equation, solve it, and interpret the result in context. Working backward can also undo a known sequence of operations.

21269.title: Elementary Algebra
21269.heading: Elementary Algebra > Overview Chapter > Quadratic equations
21269.content:
[[Quadratic Equations]] studies equations whose highest power of the unknown is two. Standard form places all terms on one side as (ax^2 + bx + c = 0), with (a\neq0). When the quadratic factors, the zero-product property converts one equation into separate linear equations: if a product is zero, at least one factor must be zero.

Completing the square turns (x^2 + bx) into a perfect-square trinomial by adding ((b/2)^2). The quadratic formula generalizes this method and gives solutions even when convenient integer factorization is unavailable. Some equations that initially contain fractions or higher-looking structures can be rearranged into quadratic form. Regardless of method, each candidate solution should be checked against the original equation and any restrictions introduced by denominators.

21270.title: Elementary Algebra
21270.heading: Elementary Algebra > Overview Chapter > Inequalities and intervals
21270.content:
[[Linear Inequalities and Intervals]] replaces equality with an ordering relation. Adding the same quantity to both sides preserves the relation, as does multiplying by a positive quantity. Multiplication or division by a negative quantity reverses the direction because it reflects positions across zero on the number line.

An inequality generally describes a solution set rather than a single value. Intervals provide a compact way to represent consecutive portions of the real line. Open endpoints exclude a boundary and closed endpoints include it; intervals may be bounded on both sides or extend without bound. Compound inequalities combine constraints through intersection or union. Graphing the result makes endpoint inclusion and direction visible, while a word problem determines whether phrases such as "at least," "no more than," or "between" require strict or inclusive boundaries.

Across these topics, elementary algebra is a discipline of preserving relationships while changing form. Arithmetic properties justify each rewrite, symbolic notation exposes general structure, and verification checks that a transformation still answers the original question. This foundation supports later mathematics because it makes abstraction operational: a relationship can be represented, manipulated, tested, and reused beyond the particular numbers that first revealed it.

21281.sourceSearchName: domain driven design domain driven design
21281.title: Domain-Driven Design
21281.heading: Domain-Driven Design > Overview Chapter
21281.content:
Domain-Driven Design begins before code. [[Domain Discovery and Ubiquitous Language]] separates the problem a business is trying to solve from the technical solution chosen to solve it. The problem space contains current and desired states, constraints, and business rules; the solution space contains the software structures and steps proposed in response. [[Essential Complexity]] belongs to the problem itself, while [[Accidental Complexity]] is introduced by frameworks, databases, integration choices, and other solution mechanisms. This distinction keeps architectural machinery from being mistaken for business value. Teams reduce uncertainty through [[Domain Knowledge]] and [[Knowledge Crunching]], gathering information from multiple experts and testing their assumptions. The resulting [[Ubiquitous Language]] must be used consistently in conversation, code, tests, interfaces, and data within one context. When a term changes meaning, the team has found evidence of a contextual boundary rather than a reason to force one universal definition.

[[EventStorming Collaborative Modeling]] turns that learning into a visible, participatory model. Participants first record [[Domain Event]]s: past-tense facts that changed the state of the business. Arranging them on an [[Event Timeline]] reveals order, concurrency, missing steps, and interactions among systems. The large modeling surface lets many people work at once instead of routing every idea through a single diagrammer. Domain experts contribute how work actually happens, while developers and other participants ask questions that expose assumptions. An [[EventStorming Hotspot]] marks disagreement or missing knowledge so the workshop can continue without pretending the uncertainty has been resolved. External systems are shown explicitly because events can cross organizational or technical control boundaries. The model is temporary by design, but its discoveries guide vocabulary, scope, prototypes, and follow-up investigation.

The discoveries become software through [[Domain Model Building Blocks]]. A [[Domain Model]] represents a proposed solution using the concepts and behavior of the domain; it is not merely a database schema. An [[Anemic Domain Model]] separates data from the rules that operate on it, making behavior difficult to locate and understand. A [[Domain Entity]] is tracked by identity through change, whereas a [[Value Object]] is defined by its values and can validate a domain-specific type before it enters an entity. A [[Domain Object Factory]] creates valid domain objects when construction requires named rules or conversion. A [[Domain Service]] expresses domain behavior that does not naturally belong to one entity while keeping infrastructure implementations outside the model. [[Entity Invariant]]s prevent behavior from leaving an entity in an invalid state, and event-applied transitions keep the fact of change coupled to the state it produces.
links: Software Design Patterns and Application Architecture
CQRS Query and Read Model Design

21282.sourceSearchName: domain driven design domain driven design
21282.title: Domain-Driven Design
21282.heading: Domain-Driven Design > Overview Chapter
21282.content:
[[Application Commands and Service Boundaries]] connect that model to the outside world without allowing delivery and infrastructure concerns to take it over. [[Domain Model Isolation]] keeps persistence, transport, serialization, and user-interface mechanisms outside the core. A [[Public API Contract]] describes serialized requests with stable boundary types such as a [[Data Transfer Object]]. An [[Application Command]] expresses an actor's intent to change state, while a [[Command Handler]] or [[Application Service]] loads the relevant model, invokes its behavior, and persists the result. HTTP is one possible delivery mechanism, not part of the domain itself. This separation allows the model to be tested in memory and lets transport or persistence choices evolve without rewriting the business rules.

[[Aggregate Consistency and Persistence]] defines where atomic business correctness is required. An [[Aggregate]] is a small group of entities and value objects that changes as one consistency unit. Its [[Aggregate Root]] is the only entry point exposed to callers and protects rules spanning the aggregate. The aggregate boundary is also a [[Transaction Boundary]]: an operation either leaves the whole aggregate valid or leaves it unchanged. Other aggregates are referenced by identity rather than held in one enormous object graph. [[Optimistic Concurrency]] detects whether another command changed an aggregate after it was read. The [[Repository Pattern]] abstracts loading and saving aggregate state, and a [[Unit of Work]] coordinates the persistence commit. These abstractions do not remove [[Persistence Impedance Mismatch]]; document serializers and relational mappings can still pressure a domain model to adopt storage-specific shapes, so those compromises must remain visible.

Writes and reads often need different shapes. [[CQRS Query and Read Model Design]] separates state-changing commands from information-returning queries. [[Command Query Responsibility Segregation]] can begin within one application and one database; it does not require separate services or storage. A repository serves aggregate behavior on the command side, but an [[Application Query]] can retrieve a purpose-built [[Read Model]] directly. This avoids forcing cross-aggregate display needs through a single aggregate repository. Read models should use the same domain language as the user decision they support and may combine data from several aggregates. The [[Read-to-Write Mismatch]] explains why indexing and normalization choices that favor writes can make reads awkward, and vice versa. CQRS accepts that asymmetry rather than stretching one representation across incompatible jobs.

[[Event Sourcing and Projections]] changes persistence from storing the latest snapshot to storing the facts that produced it. In [[Event Sourcing]], new domain events are appended to an [[Event Stream]], normally one stream per aggregate. An [[Event Store]] preserves their order and lets the application rebuild an [[Event-Sourced Aggregate]] by folding those events through its transition function. This [[Aggregate Rehydration]] makes history the source of truth and supports auditing and replay, but it also creates new operational responsibilities. A [[Projection]] consumes events to build query-oriented models. A [[Catch-Up Subscription]] processes history before switching to live events, while a [[Projection Checkpoint]] records the last successfully processed position. The separation makes read models rebuildable but commonly introduces [[Eventual Consistency]] between a committed event and the projections that have not yet processed it.
links: Software Design Patterns and Application Architecture
CQRS Query and Read Model Design

21283.sourceSearchName: domain driven design domain driven design
21283.title: Domain-Driven Design
21283.heading: Domain-Driven Design > Overview Chapter
21283.content:
Finally, [[Bounded Context and Organizational Design]] prevents a complex organization from collapsing into one ambiguous model. A [[Bounded Context]] establishes the boundary within which a model and its language are internally consistent. The [[Single Model Trap]] appears when one representation is forced to serve unrelated business capabilities, usually accumulating conflicting meanings and rates of change. Left unchecked, that produces a [[Big Ball of Mud]]. [[Linguistic Boundary]] analysis finds places where the same word carries different meanings; a [[Context Map]] then records contexts and their relationships. Boundaries also shape work. [[Conway's Law]] predicts that architecture will reflect communication structures, so business-aligned teams need clear [[Bounded Context Ownership]]. [[Work in Progress Limit]]s reduce queues and context switching, while [[Loose Coupling and High Alignment]] lets teams coordinate on outcomes without sharing every internal implementation decision.

Together, these practices keep software aligned with what people are trying to accomplish. The strategic practices discover language and boundaries; the tactical practices encode behavior and consistency; CQRS and event sourcing provide optional structures for asymmetric or historical data; and organizational ownership keeps those boundaries workable over time. None of the patterns is valuable merely because it has a name. Each earns its place by reducing ambiguity, protecting a real rule, or allowing a team to change one part of the system without destabilizing the rest.

21301.sourceSearchName: direct electricity conversion direct electricity conversion
21301.title: Direct Electricity Conversion
21301.heading: Direct Electricity Conversion > Overview Chapter
21301.content:
Conventional thermal power plants usually turn fuel or nuclear heat into a hot working fluid, expand that fluid through a turbine or engine, and drive an electrical generator. Each stage has its own losses, while a heat-engine cycle is bounded by the source and sink temperatures. The methods collected here change the conversion path. They may still need a heat source, reactants, a magnetic field, or an electronic power-conditioning stage, but the electrical output arises in a cell, semiconductor junction, conducting fluid, or electron gap rather than from the shaft of a prime mover. The source distinguishes six complementary approaches: [[Photovoltaic Cell Physics]], [[Photovoltaic Power Systems]], [[Fuel Cell Technologies]], [[Magnetohydrodynamic Generation]], [[Thermoelectric Power Generation]], and [[Thermionic Power Generation]]. Their differences matter more than the shared absence of a rotating generator.

[[Photovoltaic Cell Physics]] begins with the energy carried by incident photons and the allowed energy states of electrons in a solid. In a semiconductor, a forbidden band separates the valence and conduction bands. Controlled impurities produce p-type and n-type regions, and their junction establishes an electric field. A photon that can create an electron-hole pair gives the junction charge carriers that can be separated and collected. The available current depends on incident photon flux and receiving area; the voltage and conversion losses depend on the material and cell design. Long-wavelength photons may lack enough energy to cross the gap, while energy above the useful threshold can be lost as heat. This explains why increasing illumination alone does not remove the spectral and material limits on a solar cell.

[[Photovoltaic Power Systems]] turns individual cells into useful supplies. Series connections raise voltage, parallel connections raise current, and enclosed modules are assembled into larger arrays. The power system is therefore not just a junction: it also includes wiring, control, conversion, and sometimes storage or backup generation. An autonomous plant balances solar output against local demand, battery discharge, and standby generation. The designer must know the site's daily radiation, expected load, module performance, and storage requirement before choosing array area and battery capacity. Tilt and orientation affect when sunlight is collected. Cell, module, and array efficiency differ because exposed spaces, electrical resistance, temperature, and mismatch add losses as the system is scaled up.

[[Fuel Cell Technologies]] uses an electrochemical reaction rather than sunlight. Hydrogen and oxygen can combine to produce water while electrons move through an external load. The electrolyte transports ions between electrodes but should remain chemically balanced during operation. Gibbs free energy sets the maximum reversible electrical work and cell voltage, while reaction enthalpy includes the energy that cannot all become electrical output. A real cell loses voltage as current density rises: electrode reaction barriers, internal resistance, and insufficient reactant or ion transport create different forms of polarization. Fuel-cell families choose different fuels and electrolytes. Polymer-membrane cells can respond quickly at relatively low temperature, while solid-oxide and molten-carbonate cells use hotter operating conditions that can support combined heat-and-power applications.

21302.sourceSearchName: direct electricity conversion direct electricity conversion
21302.title: Direct Electricity Conversion
21302.heading: Direct Electricity Conversion > Overview Chapter
21302.content:
[[Magnetohydrodynamic Generation]] uses a fast electrically conducting fluid as the moving conductor in Faraday's induction principle. A hot gas must be ionized enough to conduct, accelerated through a duct, and passed across a strong magnetic field; electrodes collect the resulting direct current. The source separates Faraday and Hall current arrangements, open combustion-gas paths, and closed paths with recirculating inert gas or liquid metal. Seeding with easily ionized material can raise conductivity without making the gas hotter than structural materials can tolerate. The same gas, however, slows and cools as power is extracted, so its conductivity and recoverable electrical output eventually decline. That makes the MHD channel a candidate topping stage whose remaining heat can feed a conventional bottoming cycle.

[[Thermoelectric Power Generation]] makes electrical potential from a temperature difference across dissimilar conducting or semiconducting elements. The Seebeck effect produces the voltage; the related Peltier and Thomson effects describe reversible heat interchange when current flows; Joule heating is an irreversible resistance loss. A practical generator combines p-type and n-type legs between hot and cold junctions. Its performance depends on a large Seebeck response, low electrical resistance, and low unwanted thermal conduction. These properties compete, so material selection is expressed through a figure of merit rather than any one property alone. Thermopiles connect many pairs to increase voltage, and cascaded stages can use the rejected heat of one temperature range as the input to another.

[[Thermionic Power Generation]] releases electrons from a sufficiently hot emitter into a vacuum or conductive vapor gap. A cooler collector receives them, and the external circuit returns them to the emitter through a load. Emission depends strongly on temperature and surface work function; the cloud of electrons in the gap can create a space-charge barrier that hinders further transport. Cesium vapor is one way the source describes reducing that barrier. Boiler tubes and reactor fuel elements are possible hot-side integrations, but high emitter temperature, corrosion protection, collector materials, and gap control complicate the device. Unlike photovoltaic and fuel-cell conversion, this is explicitly a heat-to-work process with a thermal efficiency ceiling.

Together, these child topics show why “direct” does not mean lossless or interchangeable. A photovoltaic junction is constrained by illumination and electron-band behavior; a fuel cell by chemical free energy and transport losses; an MHD duct by gas conductivity and magnetic-field engineering; a thermoelectric pair by coupled electrical and thermal material properties; and a thermionic gap by surface emission and space charge. Their common engineering question is where energy quality is lost between source and usable electrical output. Reading the child notes in that order moves from electronic prerequisites to device behavior, then to the system arrangements needed to deliver dependable power.

21307.sourceSearchName: digital image forensics digital image forensics
21307.title: Digital Image Forensics
21307.heading: Digital Image Forensics > Overview Chapter
21307.content:
Digital image forensics asks whether the history claimed for a photograph is compatible with the evidence preserved inside it. A digital image is not produced in one step. Light first interacts with the scene, travels through the camera's optics, reaches a sensor, is converted into samples, passes through device-specific processing, and is finally encoded in a file. Editing, recompression, publication, and online sharing add further transformations. Each stage can leave regularities, and tampering may disturb them. The field therefore works backward from the available file, comparing its metadata, visible content, pixel statistics, and encoding artifacts with models of how an unaltered photograph should have formed.

[[Image Authenticity and Forensic Reasoning]] establishes how those tests should be interpreted. Authentication is not a mathematical proof that nothing happened to a file; it is a failure to find tampering with the suitable techniques that were applied. A positive result may reveal a specific edit, or it may show only that an image was resaved. A negative result is more informative when a high-quality, high-resolution file retains rich evidence than when heavy compression, resizing, or stripped metadata have destroyed it. [[Image Provenance]] can be investigated through reverse search and internal traces, but incomplete indexes and editable records make corroboration essential. Combining independent tests increases confidence, while explicit assumptions and the possibility of deliberate countermeasures keep the conclusion appropriately bounded.

[[Image Metadata and JPEG Signatures]] studies information around the pixels. EXIF directories may record the device, lens, exposure, time, position, software history, and an embedded thumbnail. An analyst can compare those claims with the visible scene and with one another. The JPEG file itself also records choices made by an encoder: quantization tables, thumbnail dimensions and processing, and marker-segment packaging may characterize a camera type or editing application. A contradiction can rule out a claimed origin, but a match cannot prove it because metadata can be rewritten and encoding conventions can be shared or deliberately copied.

[[Exposure and Lighting Forensics]] moves from file records to physical scene behavior. Aperture, shutter speed, and ISO jointly determine exposure while producing different depth-of-field, motion-blur, and noise effects. Their recorded values should be plausible for the photograph. Illumination adds further constraints. A camera flash creates characteristic falloff and direction, cast shadows imply projected light positions, planar reflections require a consistent mirror geometry, and lens flare can constrain the location of a bright source. These cues are powerful precisely because a pasted object must fit the lighting of the whole scene, yet multiple lights, unusual surfaces, and unknown motion mean that the appropriate physical model must be chosen carefully.
links: Camera Sensor and Synthetic Image Forensics

21308.sourceSearchName: digital image forensics digital image forensics
21308.title: Digital Image Forensics
21308.heading: Digital Image Forensics > Overview Chapter
21308.content:
[[Photogrammetric Image Analysis]] uses perspective geometry to connect the two-dimensional image to possible three-dimensional scenes. The pinhole camera model explains apparent scale, focal length, field of view, and the fundamental ambiguity that every image point represents a ray of possible depths. Parallel lines define vanishing points, coplanar directions define vanishing lines, and three mutually perpendicular directions can locate the camera's principal point. The same projective structure supports planar rectification and more elaborate facial or scene reconstruction. Additional constraints such as known dimensions, body articulation, contact points, and surface orientation can expose a composite that would require an implausible camera, object size, or pose.

[[JPEG Compression Forensics]] treats file encoding as a historical trace. JPEG converts color into luminance and chrominance, divides channels into blocks, transforms those blocks into spatial frequencies, quantizes coefficients, and encodes the result. This ordinary process creates blocking and ringing that must not be confused with manipulation. It also makes prior saves detectable. Recompression at several candidate qualities can reveal a region with a different effective quality as a JPEG ghost. When two saves use different quantization steps, periodic holes and peaks may appear in transform-coefficient histograms. These findings demonstrate incompatible compression histories, though they do not by themselves explain why the image was resaved.

[[Copy-Move and Resampling Forensics]] addresses pixel operations used during editing. Copy-move forgery duplicates material within one photograph, often inheriting the source's color and noise well enough to blend naturally. A detector reduces an otherwise enormous search by finding salient corners, describing their local gradients, matching similar descriptors, and grouping matches that share a translation, rotation, or scale. Pixel-level verification then separates a coherent clone from ordinary repeated structures. Scaling or rotating any inserted region also requires interpolation. That resampling creates periodic local correlations which may remain measurable even when no visual artifact is obvious, although global resizing is a benign source of the same class of trace.

[[Camera Sensor and Synthetic Image Forensics]] examines evidence nearest to capture and evidence that may be absent when no camera captured the scene at all. A color filter array measures only one color at each sensor location, and demosaicing estimates the missing channels, producing periodic correlations that local editing can disrupt. Stable photo-response non-uniformity creates a fingerprint capable of linking an image to one physical sensor, while local noise differences can expose compositing or processing. Generated faces and scenes may omit these camera traces or biological signals such as subtle pulse-driven facial color changes. Such detectors remain part of a moving contest: once a missing regularity becomes known, synthesis systems can be trained to imitate it.
links: Camera Sensor and Synthetic Image Forensics

21309.sourceSearchName: digital image forensics digital image forensics
21309.title: Digital Image Forensics
21309.heading: Digital Image Forensics > Overview Chapter
21309.content: Taken together, the chapter's methods turn authenticity into a structured comparison between a claimed history and many independent consequences of that history. The strongest analysis begins with the least altered available file, selects tests whose assumptions fit its content and format, distinguishes ordinary processing from deceptive alteration, and reports both positive evidence and limitations. No technique makes photographs self-authenticating, but converging physical, geometric, statistical, and file-structural evidence can make an unsupported story increasingly difficult to sustain.

21326.sourceSearchName: data science frontiers data science frontiers
21326.title: Data Science Frontiers
21326.heading: Data Science Frontiers > Overview Chapter
21326.content:
Data science is not only a collection of algorithms. It is a chain of decisions about what may be collected, how information is represented, what a model can legitimately infer, who may control or reuse the result, and how evidence becomes action. The subjects below connect that chain from legal rules and privacy theory through text analysis, business analytics, recommendation, preprocessing, causal reasoning, and healthcare. Together they show that useful analysis depends on both computational technique and defensible governance.

[[Big Data Law and Individual Rights]] begins with the legal status of information about people. Big-data analysis makes familiar principles such as consent, purpose limitation, and data minimization harder to apply because useful correlations may appear only after collection. An apparently anonymous record can be reidentified through linkage, and nonsensitive fields can support sensitive inferences. Protection therefore cannot stop at direct identifiers. It must consider data subjects, groups affected by profiling, discriminatory outcomes, and impact assessment across an entire processing environment.

[[Automated Information Governance]] broadens the legal view from datasets to activities and sectors. Government, industry, science, and connected devices may collect, process, store, distribute, and act on information in different ways. Legal significance depends on the content and consequences of these operations, not simply on data volume or speed. Veracity matters when automated findings are treated as evidence, while cross-border systems expose differences among national and regional rules. Accountability must follow the complete automated process, including physical systems that turn information into action.

[[Privacy Theory and Legal Limits]] asks why privacy should constrain a legal order at all. The chapter uses legal positivism and the distinction between primary and secondary rules to explain how a system recognizes, changes, and adjudicates law. It then treats privacy as an intrinsic limit connected to autonomy and positive freedom rather than merely as one optional rule among others. On this view, some protected space is necessary for people to form intentions and conduct their lives even when extensive observation would be technically possible.

[[Data Ownership and Access Rights]] examines whether property-like control can solve problems of access and value. Data are nonrivalrous, can be copied without depriving the original holder, and often gain value through aggregation. These characteristics complicate ordinary ownership models. The analysis weighs market failure, labor, personality, fairness, transaction costs, externalities, attribution, collective claims, scope, publicity, and contractual control. It also stresses that personal and nonpersonal data cannot always be separated cleanly because attribution may change as new information is combined.
links: Big Data Law and Individual Rights

21327.sourceSearchName: data science frontiers data science frontiers
21327.title: Data Science Frontiers
21327.heading: Data Science Frontiers > Overview Chapter
21327.content:
[[Text Analytics Philosophy and Methods]] shows why unstructured natural language cannot be reduced safely to word counts alone. Text data mining, tokenization, bag-of-words representations, and automated content analysis make large collections tractable, but removing order and context can remove meaning. Corpus linguistics, marker sets, proximity analysis, and validation reconnect quantitative measurement with qualitative interpretation. The research question, corpus, linguistic variation, and assumptions behind a query determine what the resulting numbers can support.

[[Mobile Commerce Privacy Behavior]] follows personal information through mobile services. Dataveillance and datafication make ordinary behavior measurable, while advertising systems and data brokers combine records across applications. Consumers may express concern yet still disclose information for convenience, status, access, or monetary benefits, producing a privacy paradox. Trust, boundary management, disclosure notices, and the AdChoices icon attempt to make this exchange legible, but their value depends on whether people can understand and control what follows.

[[Evidence-Based Data Decisions]] connects raw records to organizational judgment. Extraction, transformation, loading, integration, cleaning, storage, exploration, and visualization are not neutral preliminaries; they determine what evidence becomes visible. Volume is useful only when the data are sufficiently relevant, timely, and trustworthy for the decision. A data-driven culture therefore requires both technical pipelines and a process that embeds results into actual choices rather than treating analysis as an isolated report.

[[Automated Business Analytics]] places machine learning within the Industry 4.0 and Web 4.0 vision of highly connected, adaptive systems. Business intelligence and analytics 4.0 aims to support or automate optimal decisions, but organizations also need people who can translate between analytical results and domain needs. Deep, reinforcement, and ensemble learning supply different learning mechanisms. The chapter's forecasting framework combines reinforcement learning with wavelet decomposition and thresholding, illustrating how an automated method can join signal processing, optimization, and out-of-sample evaluation.

[[Recommender System Evolution]] traces personalized prediction from memory-based collaborative filtering to model-based, content-based, hybrid, and large-scale latent-factor systems. Matrix factorization represents users and items through compact factors, while alternating least squares supports scalable estimation. Distributed frameworks make much larger datasets tractable, but scale does not eliminate questions about evaluation, context, changing preferences, user experience, or streaming updates. A recommendation is ultimately an intervention in what a person sees, not merely a high score.
links: Big Data Law and Individual Rights

21328.sourceSearchName: data science frontiers data science frontiers
21328.title: Data Science Frontiers
21328.heading: Data Science Frontiers > Overview Chapter
21328.content:
[[Big Data Preprocessing]] focuses on the choices that make high-dimensional analysis feasible. Discretization converts continuous values into intervals, while feature selection retains informative variables and removes weak or redundant ones. Filter, wrapper, and embedded models use different relationships with the eventual learner. Feature subsets and rankings answer different questions, and the search space grows exponentially. Parallel minimum-description-length discretization, minimum-redundancy maximum-relevance selection, and distributed methods address scale while preserving interpretability and stability as design concerns.

[[Causal Inference Philosophy]] challenges the claim that abundant correlations make causation unnecessary. Enumerative induction relies on repetition, whereas eliminative and variational induction examine what changes when circumstances vary. The method of difference motivates causal rules that distinguish manipulable or predictively useful relationships from accidental correlations. Probability also needs an interpretation: the chapter develops an objective account grounded in causal symmetries and independence. Data-driven inquiry can remain inductive without pretending that facts interpret themselves.

[[Chinese Healthcare Big Data]] applies the full chain to hospitals, public-health institutions, regional platforms, insurance systems, and personal devices. These sources can support health management, infectious-disease prediction, cost control, and analysis of drug use. They also contain inconsistent codes, biased or erroneous records, commercial sensitivities, and deeply personal information. Regulation of acquisition and cross-border flows, privacy remedies, and mechanisms for sharing and opening resources are therefore part of the analytical infrastructure rather than external obstacles to it.

Across these areas, the central frontier is coordination. A technically strong model can still fail when its data were collected for another purpose, its categories erase context, its correlations are mistaken for causes, its outputs cannot be integrated into a decision, or its use violates legitimate expectations. Conversely, governance without an understanding of processing cannot identify where risks and opportunities arise. Data science becomes dependable when representation, computation, interpretation, law, and institutional action are designed as connected parts of one system.
links: Big Data Law and Individual Rights

21343.sourceSearchName: data clustering algorithms data clustering algorithms
21343.title: Data Clustering Algorithms
21343.heading: Data Clustering Algorithms > Overview Chapter
21343.content:
Clustering is not one algorithm but a family of ways to define and recover structure. [[Cluster Analysis Foundations]] supplies the common vocabulary: objects are represented by features, a proximity or probabilistic model expresses resemblance, and an objective or structural criterion determines what counts as a useful group. That framing matters because the same records can support several legitimate clusterings. A method that seeks compact spherical groups answers a different question from one that seeks dense regions, graph communities, correlated subspaces, or alternate views. Modern clustering therefore begins by matching the representation and algorithm to the geometry, scale, and intended interpretation of the data.

[[Unsupervised Feature Selection for Clustering]] moves feature choice inside that unsupervised problem. Without class labels, relevance must be inferred from neighborhood preservation, spectral structure, sparsity, or the quality of clusters induced by a feature subset. Filter methods score features independently of a final clusterer, wrapper methods evaluate subsets through clustering performance, and hybrid methods combine both. Feature weighting can also let a clustering procedure suppress irrelevant dimensions while it estimates groups. These methods are especially important because noise dimensions can overwhelm meaningful proximity before an algorithm ever begins grouping points.

Two classical algorithm families illustrate how different structural assumptions lead to different outputs. [[Partition and K-Means Clustering]] assigns every object to one of a fixed number of groups and typically optimizes dispersion around representative centers. It is efficient and scalable, but sensitive to initialization, outliers, and non-spherical structure. [[Hierarchical Clustering Methods]] instead builds nested partitions by repeated merges or splits. Linkage rules determine which geometry the hierarchy favors, and the dendrogram exposes solutions at several resolutions. Neither family is universally preferable: partitioning emphasizes a single economical summary, while hierarchy emphasizes relationships among possible resolutions.

[[Density and Grid-Based Clustering]] avoids requiring globular groups. Density methods grow clusters through connected neighborhoods of sufficiently dense points, leaving sparse observations as noise. OPTICS records a reachability ordering that reveals structure across density scales, while DENCLUE describes density through influence functions and attractors. Grid methods quantize the data space and operate on populated cells rather than individual records. STING stores statistical summaries, WaveCluster transforms the grid to expose dense regions, and CLIQUE searches dense subspaces. These techniques can recover irregular shapes and reduce data-access costs, although results still depend on resolution and density parameters.

21344.sourceSearchName: data clustering algorithms data clustering algorithms
21344.title: Data Clustering Algorithms
21344.heading: Data Clustering Algorithms > Overview Chapter
21344.content:
[[Outlier Detection and DBSCAN]] connects this density view to anomaly handling. DBSCAN distinguishes core, border, and noise points through neighborhood support, while local-density comparisons identify observations that are sparse relative to their surroundings. The same mechanisms that outline a cluster therefore also explain why some observations remain outside it.

[[Model-Based Clustering]] treats membership as inference under a data-generating model. Finite mixtures associate clusters with probability components, and expectation-maximization alternates between estimating membership probabilities and component parameters. This makes overlap, uncertainty, and covariance structure explicit, but model misspecification and local optima remain serious concerns. [[Categorical Data Clustering]] handles records for which ordinary geometric means are meaningless. Algorithms such as ROCK, STIRR, CACTUS, and CLICK replace Euclidean geometry with neighbor links, relational reinforcement, co-occurrence summaries, or graph structures derived from categorical values.

Linear-algebraic methods provide another view. [[Matrix Factorization and Spectral Clustering]] represents observations through latent nonnegative factors or eigenvectors of a similarity graph. Nonnegative matrix factorization creates additive, parts-based representations that can support both clustering and co-clustering. Spectral methods embed graph relationships in a low-dimensional eigenspace before applying a simpler partitioner. Ratio-cut and normalized-cut relaxations clarify which graph separation objective is being approximated. Their flexibility depends on a well-chosen affinity graph and on computational methods capable of extracting the needed factors or eigenvectors.

[[High-Dimensional and Subspace Clustering]] addresses the fact that distance loses contrast when many irrelevant dimensions accumulate. A group may be visible in only a subset of attributes, and different groups may occupy different subspaces. Axis-parallel methods search selected dimensions, projected methods associate each cluster with its own feature set, and correlation methods allow arbitrarily oriented manifolds. CLIQUE exploits monotonicity of dense regions, while PROCLUS and ORCLUS combine partitioning with subspace estimation. The search space is enormous, so practical methods balance coverage, redundancy, interpretability, and computational cost.

Scale and motion change the computational problem again. [[Stream and Big Data Clustering]] must summarize observations that arrive continuously or exceed one machine's memory. STREAM compresses batches into weighted representatives; BIRCH uses compact clustering-feature summaries; CluStream stores microclusters and a pyramidal history for later macroclustering. DenStream and D-Stream adapt density ideas to evolving data, and HPStream combines fading summaries with projected dimensions. Distributed approaches partition work across processors or MapReduce stages, but a scalable implementation must still preserve enough statistics to support a meaningful global solution.

21345.sourceSearchName: data clustering algorithms data clustering algorithms
21345.title: Data Clustering Algorithms
21345.heading: Data Clustering Algorithms > Overview Chapter
21345.content:
[[Scalable Hierarchical Search]] uses a more direct route to some large-data hierarchies: fixed-precision digit or hash codes can place nearby observations in shared prefix buckets. The Baire longest-common-prefix distance and m-adic tree convert an ordered code into nested groups; under bounded code length, insertion can be linear in the number of records. The chosen measurement precision therefore sets the visible cluster resolution. Random projections can create such codes for high-dimensional observations, but the projections and bins are approximations whose stability requires checking. Triangle-based ultrametricity measures and consensus seriation probe whether a hierarchy is supported rather than merely imposed. The book also uses factor-space distance identities and clusterwise redshift regression to illustrate how geometric shortcuts and local modeling can reduce computation without losing sight of domain interpretation.

Specialized data types require specialized representations. [[Document and Multimedia Clustering]] works with sparse word vectors, snippets, microblogs, images, faces, and video stories. Text methods must handle extreme sparsity, document length, and background knowledge; multimedia methods must bridge low-level features and semantic concepts. Visual words, temporal segmentation, and multimodal fusion turn raw signals into objects that clustering can compare. [[Time-Series and Biological Clustering]] must additionally respect order, alignment, correlation, and domain structure. Dynamic time warping aligns sequences with differing pace, trajectory methods compare paths, and biclustering or triclustering finds coherent gene-expression patterns across subsets of genes, conditions, and time.

Relations among objects can be primary data rather than a side effect of feature construction. [[Network and Uncertain Data Clustering]] includes graph bisection, multilevel partitioning, Markov flow, hypergraph models, overlapping communities, and clustering when each value is a distribution or set of possible worlds. Network objectives balance cut size against community cohesion. Uncertain-data methods propagate uncertainty into distances, density reachability, centroids, or expected objectives instead of collapsing every object to a single point. Both cases warn against forcing relational or probabilistic information into an ordinary flat table too early.

Human knowledge can guide the search without fully supervising it. [[Interactive and Semi-Supervised Clustering]] allows analysts to steer a visualization, choose among nearby solutions, provide seed labels, or state must-link and cannot-link constraints. Graph cuts, label propagation, and learned embeddings can spread limited guidance through the data. Interaction is useful when quality includes domain meaning that no internal index captures, but it also makes provenance important: the final grouping should record which constraints and interventions shaped it.

21346.sourceSearchName: data clustering algorithms data clustering algorithms
21346.title: Data Clustering Algorithms
21346.heading: Data Clustering Algorithms > Overview Chapter
21346.content:
A dataset may also contain several defensible organizations. [[Alternative and Ensemble Clustering]] either seeks a substantially different view from an existing solution or combines many candidate partitions into a consensus. Alternative clustering can use explicit constraints, orthogonality, or information-theoretic objectives to avoid rediscovering the same structure. Ensemble methods work from co-association, voting, probabilistic combination, or consensus optimization. Diversity among inputs is valuable only when the component solutions retain useful signal; otherwise an ensemble can merely stabilize shared error.

[[C++ Clustering Software Design]] connects these mathematical families to reusable implementation. It models datasets, distances, clusters, arguments, algorithm lifecycles, and results as cooperating C++ abstractions, then uses design patterns to keep shared control flow separate from method-specific computation. Its implementations of hierarchical, partitional, fuzzy, model-based, genetic, subspace, and parallel algorithms show how software architecture can make experiments consistent without erasing the distinctive mathematics of each method.

Finally, [[Cluster Validity and Simulation]] determines whether the output deserves interpretation. External measures compare clusters with known labels, internal measures balance cohesion and separation, and relative measures compare algorithms or parameter choices. Pair-counting, information-theoretic, silhouette, stability, and Monte Carlo procedures illuminate different failure modes. No single score can certify that a clustering is true. Validation must connect the algorithm's assumptions, the chosen representation, perturbation behavior, and the application purpose. Together, these topics form a disciplined workflow: select informative structure, choose an algorithm whose biases fit it, preserve uncertainty and scale where necessary, and test whether the discovered organization remains useful under credible alternatives.

21348.title: Data Classification
21348.heading: Data Classification
21348.content:
Parent topic: [[Machine Learning and Neural Networks]]

Data classification learns a mapping from measured features to known category labels and then applies that mapping to unseen observations. The subject is broader than any single algorithm: successful classification depends on representation, training data, inductive assumptions, computational scale, evaluation, and the structure of the domain. Full Notes link to the focused child topics below rather than directly to this chapter tag.

21349.title: Data Classification
21349.heading: Data Classification > Overview Chapter
21349.content:
[[Classification Feature Selection]] begins before a classifier is fitted. High-dimensional collections often contain noisy, irrelevant, or redundant variables that increase cost and encourage overfitting. Filters score variables without repeatedly fitting a chosen classifier, wrappers judge candidate subsets through predictive performance, and embedded methods select variables during model fitting. Structured and streaming settings add group, tree, graph, or arrival-order constraints. The governing idea is to retain a small, interpretable subset that preserves discrimination between classes.

[[Probabilistic Classification Models]] express a prediction through probabilities, likelihoods, or graphical dependencies. Naive Bayes deliberately simplifies the joint distribution with conditional-independence assumptions, while logistic regression models conditional class probability directly. Bayesian networks, hidden Markov models, Markov random fields, and conditional random fields represent different dependency structures. These models clarify what evidence contributes to a class score and whether the task calls for generating observations, estimating a boundary, or performing inference over connected variables.

[[Classification and Decision Trees]] organizes prediction as recursive partitioning. Each internal node tests a feature, each branch represents an outcome, and each leaf supplies a class decision. Split criteria seek purer child nodes, while stopping and pruning control unnecessary complexity. Trees are readable because a root-to-leaf path is an explicit decision rule, but their apparent simplicity conceals important choices about continuous values, missing observations, scalability, and protection against fitting accidental patterns in the training sample.

[[Rule and Instance-Based Classification]] contrasts two ways to make the decision explicit. Rule learners induce ordered or unordered if-then conditions whose antecedents describe a region and whose consequents name a class. Instance-based methods postpone generalization until prediction time, using nearby stored examples and a distance function to infer a label. Rules favor global descriptions; lazy methods favor local adaptation. Both depend on conflict resolution, relevance weighting, and careful definitions of similarity or coverage.

[[Support Vector Classification]] frames classification as geometric separation. A linear support vector machine chooses a boundary with a large margin from the closest training observations, and slack variables trade margin width against violations when the classes overlap. Kernels replace ordinary inner products so that nonlinear boundaries can be learned implicitly in a transformed feature space. Dual optimization concentrates the solution on support vectors, while one-versus-rest and one-versus-one decompositions extend the binary formulation to multiple classes.

21350.title: Data Classification
21350.heading: Data Classification > Overview Chapter
21350.content:
[[Neural Network Classification and Clustering]] builds nonlinear decision functions from connected computational units. Threshold, linear, sigmoid, and radial-basis units differ in their response, while feedforward topology determines how intermediate representations are composed. Perceptron and delta-style updates establish the basic learning logic; multilayer networks use backpropagation to distribute output error across hidden layers. Competitive and self-organizing systems add an unsupervised view, showing how learned representations can support both class separation and structure discovery.

[[Streaming and Scalable Classification]] changes the engineering assumptions. A stream may be too large to retain and may evolve through concept drift, so a useful classifier must update incrementally while forgetting stale evidence. Rare or novel classes are especially difficult because recent windows contain few examples. For large stored collections, scalable SVM solvers, parallel decision-tree construction, sparse computation, and distributed model combination reduce training cost without changing the predictive objective.

[[Text and Multimedia Classification]] adapts general methods to representations with distinctive structure. Text is sparse and high-dimensional, making word selection and frequency modeling central. Images, audio, and video require feature extraction before learning, and multimedia decisions can fuse signals at the feature or decision level. Ontological and geographic relations contribute context that isolated low-level features miss. The classifier therefore depends as much on an appropriate representation and fusion strategy as on the final prediction rule.

[[Sequence and Network Classification]] retains dependencies that ordinary feature vectors discard. Time-series methods compare trajectories despite shifts or unequal timing, while discrete-sequence methods use patterns, alignments, kernels, or generative models. Network classification exploits edges between cases: labels can propagate, neighbors can become relational features, and repeated local inference can produce a collective assignment. These methods must avoid treating correlated observations as independent while still finding a computationally manageable representation.

[[Uncertain and Rare-Class Classification]] addresses two departures from clean, balanced training data. Uncertain attributes are distributions or ranges rather than exact points, requiring split, rule, density, or neighborhood calculations to integrate measurement uncertainty. Rare-class tasks assign asymmetric importance to the minority class through costs, weights, resampling, or one-class models. Positive-unlabeled and novelty-detection settings further weaken label availability, so evaluation must distinguish genuine detection from superficially high accuracy caused by the dominant class.

21351.title: Data Classification
21351.heading: Data Classification > Overview Chapter
21351.content:
[[Distance Metric Learning]] treats similarity itself as a supervised parameter. A generalized Mahalanobis metric is equivalent to Euclidean distance after a learned projection, so its matrix determines which directions count as close. Class labels or must-link and cannot-link constraints encourage same-class cases to approach one another and different-class cases to separate. Global, local, linear, nonlinear, batch, semi-supervised, and online variants tailor this geometry to the downstream neighborhood decision.

[[Ensemble and Semi-Supervised Classification]] obtains additional evidence in two different ways. Ensembles combine diverse models so that uncorrelated errors can cancel, using Bayesian weighting, bootstrap aggregation, random forests, boosting, or stacked predictions. Semi-supervised methods combine labeled and unlabeled cases under assumptions about shared distributions, multiple views, smooth graph neighborhoods, or cluster structure. Both approaches improve generalization only when their extra components contribute information rather than repeating the same bias.

[[Transfer and Active Learning]] manages scarce labels strategically. Transfer learning reuses instances, representations, parameters, or relations from a source domain, but mismatched domains can cause negative transfer. Active learning instead chooses which unlabeled case should be sent to an oracle. Uncertainty, committee disagreement, expected model change, and expected error reduction measure different kinds of prospective value. The common goal is to spend existing knowledge or labeling effort where it changes the classifier most.

[[Classification Evaluation and Visualization]] closes the loop between model construction and warranted conclusions. Holdout, cross-validation, Monte Carlo, and bootstrap schemes separate fitting from testing with different bias, variance, and computational costs. Accuracy, precision, recall, F-measure, and receiver-operating characteristics reveal different error tradeoffs, especially under imbalance. Statistical comparisons test whether performance differences recur across datasets, while visual classification systems help people inspect boundaries, uncertainty, features, and ensemble behavior.

Taken together, these topics describe classification as an evidence pipeline rather than a leaderboard of algorithms. Representations and selected features define what can be learned; model families encode different assumptions; scale and data structure determine feasible computation; auxiliary labels, transferred knowledge, and ensembles alter the information available; and evaluation determines whether an apparent improvement is trustworthy. A sound classifier aligns all of these choices with the costs, dependencies, and uncertainty of the application.

21359.title: Cybersecurity Foundations and Defense
21359.heading: Cybersecurity Foundations and Defense > Overview Chapter
21359.content:
[[Cybersecurity Goals and Trust]] defines the outcomes a security program is trying to preserve. Confidentiality restricts disclosure, integrity preserves trustworthy systems and data, and availability keeps resources usable by authorized parties. Authentication establishes an identity, authorization constrains what that identity may do, and nonrepudiation supplies evidence that an action or message came from its claimed source. These goals interact, so one flaw can undermine several of them at once.

Several of those goals depend on [[Applied Cryptography and PKI]]. Encryption translates plaintext into ciphertext under a key, symmetric cryptography handles substantial data efficiently, and asymmetric cryptography supports exchanges between parties that do not already share a secret. Hashes produce one-way fixed-size representations for integrity checks, salts distinguish password verifiers, and message authentication codes or digital signatures add evidence about origin. Public key infrastructure connects public keys to identities through certificates and certificate authorities.

Protection within a host belongs to [[Operating System Security and Access Control]]. The operating system separates users, objects, processes, and memory so one execution context cannot silently corrupt another. Physical, temporal, sandboxed, and cryptographic separation provide different strengths and costs. Mandatory, discretionary, role-based, and rule-based access controls then decide which identities may reach particular resources. These mechanisms make authorization enforceable beneath individual applications.

[[Layered Cyber Defense and Secure Development]] treats no single safeguard as sufficient. People, networks, hosts, applications, data, cloud services, and mobile devices form successive defensive boundaries, with redundant controls limiting the effect of a failure at one layer. Firewalls, detection and prevention systems, and event monitoring protect and observe network activity. Secure development moves penetration testing, code review, and architecture analysis earlier into planning, construction, and deployment instead of waiting for a completed application to reveal its weaknesses.

Defenders prioritize their effort through [[Cyber Threat Vulnerability and Risk Analysis]]. A threat describes potential harm, a vulnerability is an exploitable weakness, and risk combines threat, vulnerability, likelihood, and impact around a valued asset. Attribution asks who performed an attack and how, while vulnerability catalogs and web-risk categories provide shared names for known weaknesses. The cyber kill chain breaks an intrusion into reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, and actions on objectives so defenses can interrupt more than the final step.

21360.sourceSearchName: cybersecurity foundations and defense cybersecurity foundations and defense
21360.title: Cybersecurity Foundations and Defense
21360.heading: Cybersecurity Foundations and Defense > Overview Chapter
21360.content:
[[Malware Types and Propagation]] distinguishes malicious programs by dependence, replication, disguise, and objective. Viruses attach to hosts, worms execute and spread independently, Trojans masquerade as legitimate software, and logic bombs wait for a trigger. Bots form remotely controlled networks, while spyware, rootkits, backdoors, adware, and ransomware specialize in observation, concealment, access, unwanted advertising, or denial through extortion. Component models expose the search, copying, propagation, control, triggering, tracking, and payload stages behind those labels.

Security appears in ordinary technology through [[Everyday Cybersecurity Applications]]. Passwords, additional factors, biometrics, virtual private networks, and tokens establish or protect access. E-commerce and payment systems depend on protected identities and transaction data, while blockchains use cryptographic records to make transactions difficult to alter or deny. Smart devices and Internet of Things equipment extend the same concerns to constrained, always-connected hardware whose default credentials and long service lives can make large botnets possible.

[[Adaptive and Outcome-Based Cyber Defense]] looks beyond fixed attack signatures. Computer immunology models a system as distinguishing legitimate self from dangerous nonself, remembering earlier infections, detecting novel behavior, and protecting its own defensive mechanisms. Outcome-based defense assumes attacks may occur and focuses resources on preventing denial of service, data theft, or deception that would defeat the system's mission. Behavioral baselines, anomaly detection, extrusion detection, and preserved multi-day context support responses to changing and persistent threats.

Together, these topics connect security objectives to concrete controls and observable attack behavior. Trust is not produced by one device or algorithm: it emerges from protected identities and keys, constrained execution, layered monitoring, secure development, risk-informed priorities, informed users, and recovery mechanisms aligned with the outcomes a system exists to deliver.

21375.heading: CSS Styling and Layout > Overview Chapter
21375.content:
[[CSS Stylesheet Integration]] begins at the boundary between a document and its presentation. CSS may arrive through an external link, an embedded style element, an import rule, or an inline declaration. Each route changes where the rules live and how widely they can be reused, while the rule structure still joins selectors to declarations. Replaced elements, display roles, vendor prefixes, whitespace, and comments define the practical vocabulary in which those rules operate.

Once styles are available, [[CSS Selectors and Pseudo-Elements]] determines which document nodes they address. Element, class, ID, and attribute selectors identify content by different kinds of evidence. Combinators describe ancestry or sibling relationships, structural pseudo-classes use position within the document tree, and dynamic pseudo-classes respond to states such as hovering or focus. Pseudo-elements target generated or typographic portions that are not ordinary elements in the source document.

Matching alone does not decide the result. [[CSS Cascade and Inheritance]] resolves all declarations that can affect a property by comparing importance, origin, specificity, and source order. Inheritance can supply a value from an ancestor when the property permits it, and computed values translate the winning declaration into the form used for later layout. This ordered conflict-resolution process is the central mechanism behind the word “cascading.”

The declarations themselves draw on [[CSS Values Units and Colors]]. Keywords, strings, URLs, numbers, percentages, dimensions, resolutions, colors, and attribute-derived values have different syntactic and computational behavior. Absolute and relative units anchor measurements to different references, while `calc()` combines compatible quantities. RGB and HSL offer different descriptions of color, and custom properties provide scoped value substitution through identifiers beginning with two hyphens.

[[CSS Web Typography]] chooses and configures the fonts used to draw text. Generic families provide fallbacks, while `@font-face` describes downloadable resources and their usable ranges. Weight, size, style, stretch, kerning, variants, feature settings, synthesis, and the font shorthand all participate in font matching. The browser works through the declared family list and available faces until it finds a resource that can represent the requested text.

After a font is selected, [[CSS Text Layout and Decoration]] controls how glyphs occupy lines. Indentation and horizontal alignment shape blocks of text; line height and vertical alignment position inline boxes relative to a shared line box. Word spacing, letter spacing, transformations, decorations, and shadows alter appearance without changing the underlying document text. Whitespace, wrapping, hyphenation, writing mode, orientation, and direction determine where lines break and in which direction they progress.

21376.title: CSS Styling and Layout
21376.heading: CSS Styling and Layout > Overview Chapter
21376.content:
Every displayed element participates in [[CSS Box Model and Normal Flow]]. Content, padding, borders, and margins form nested regions whose dimensions affect surrounding boxes. Containing blocks supply reference rectangles for percentages and positioning. Block, inline, inline-block, list-item, and replaced-element formatting create different box behaviors, while width, height, margin collapsing, overflow, and visibility decide how much space a box uses and what happens when content exceeds it.

[[CSS Borders Backgrounds and Shadows]] adds visible treatment around and behind those boxes. Padding separates content from a border; margins separate one box from others; and outlines provide emphasis without consuming layout space. Borders can vary by side, use rounded corners, or draw from an image. Background layers can be positioned, sized, clipped, repeated, and combined, while linear or radial gradients generate images and box shadows simulate offset or inset depth.

Before modern layout modules, authors often relied on [[CSS Floats Positioning and Shapes]]. Floats remove a box from ordinary block flow while allowing inline content to wrap around it, and clearing prevents later boxes from wrapping beside selected floats. Shapes refine the wrap boundary beyond a rectangle. Absolute, relative, fixed, and sticky positioning instead use offsets and containing blocks, with stacking levels deciding which overlapping boxes appear in front.

[[CSS Flexible Box Layout]] creates a one-dimensional formatting context whose items are arranged along a main axis and aligned along a cross axis. Direction and wrapping establish the available flex lines. Distribution and alignment properties allocate leftover space, while the flex basis, growth factor, and shrink factor determine how item sizes respond to the container. The visual order can differ from source order, but document and accessibility order still follow the source.

[[CSS Grid Layout]] provides a two-dimensional system of rows, columns, lines, cells, and named areas. Track sizing may use fixed lengths, content-aware functions, or fractional units, and repeated patterns can generate many tracks compactly. Explicit placement and auto-placement share the same grid, while the implicit grid grows when items fall outside the declared structure. Gaps, alignment, overlap, and stacking finish the layout without requiring content order to dictate visual position.

Structured content receives additional models in [[CSS Tables Lists and Generated Content]]. Table boxes are assembled from rows, columns, groups, cells, and captions, including anonymous boxes required to repair incomplete structures. Border models, layered backgrounds, sizing, and alignment control the rendered table. Lists use markers, images, and marker positions, while generated content and counters insert presentational text or numbering without changing the source markup.

21377.title: CSS Styling and Layout

21377.content:
Time and geometry meet in [[CSS Transforms Transitions and Animation]]. Two- and three-dimensional transform functions alter an element’s rendered coordinate space around a chosen origin and perspective. Transitions interpolate a changed property between states, with duration, delay, and timing functions controlling the route. Keyframe animations explicitly define intermediate states, repetitions, direction, fill, and play state. Motion remains an enhancement and should be constrained when it could trigger vestibular or seizure-related harm.

[[CSS Filters Blending Clipping and Masking]] changes how already-laid-out content is painted and combined. Filter functions can blur, shadow, brighten, recolor, or alter contrast. Blend modes calculate interactions between element or background colors, while isolation creates a controlled compositing group. Clipping uses a hard geometric boundary, whereas masking uses image values to vary visibility. Object fitting and positioning determine how replaced content occupies its content box.

Finally, [[CSS Media Queries and Print Styling]] makes presentation conditional on output conditions. Media types and feature descriptors test characteristics such as dimensions, orientation, or resolution, and logical operators combine those tests. Feature queries separately test property-value support for progressive enhancement. Paged-media rules introduce page boxes, margins, breaks, and print-specific styles so the same document can remain intelligible on screens and on physical pages.

Together, these topics describe CSS as a staged rendering language. Rules enter the document, selectors match elements, the cascade resolves values, formatting models construct boxes and lines, layout systems arrange them, and painting features determine their final appearance. Conditional rules then adapt that result to the capabilities and medium through which the document is presented.

21439.title: Computing History
21439.heading: Computing History
21439.content:
Parent topic: [[Computer Science]]

The history of computing is not a straight succession of faster calculators. Modern computing emerged when calculation, coded information, automatic control, electronics, communication, and human interaction converged around programmable digital machines. Its development was shaped jointly by technical possibility, military and scientific demand, commercial strategy, user communities, standards, and design.
